title: Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$-States: Dynamic $|T\rangle$ Post-Selection and Budget-Aware Factory Provisioning
authors: Maxwell Poster, Sayam Sethi, Yuhao Liu, Jonathan Baker, Costin Iancu
abstract: Magic $|T\rangle$-state preparation dominates the cost of fault-tolerant quantum computation on surface codes, yet cultivation and distillation are typically provisioned statically, leaving much of the program's error budget unused. We present Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$ States (GP$|T\rangle$-S), a lattice surgery scheduler and factory allocator that co-optimizes both methods under a total $T$-error budget. GP$|T\rangle$-S uses the complementary gap of each cultivated state as a fidelity estimate and dynamically adjusts the cultivation gap cutoff, converting budget slack into speed by giving the scheduler control over the cultivation post-selection. GP$|T\rangle$-S also characterizes distillation factories by size, $|T\rangle$-state production rate, and budget slack, and introduces cultivating factories that embed cultivation within routing channels, achieving fidelities otherwise requiring two-level distillation at a single-level footprint. GP$|T\rangle$-S organizes these characterizations into a factory catalog, and performs distillation factory allocation over this catalog in tandem with the gap cutoff using dynamic-programming to achieve one of i) minimum spacetime volume, ii) minimum execution time, or iii) minimum space overhead, all within a user-provided $T$-error budget. Across sixteen benchmarks under high and low $T$-error budgets of $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-5}$ respectively, GP$|T\rangle$-S consistently outperforms cultivation-only and single-factory baselines without exceeding the budget, achieving a 5.5$\times$ geometric mean speedup in logical cycle count and a 3.4$\times$ geometric mean reduction in space-time volume.
summary: This paper introduces a novel scheduler, GP|T>S, designed to optimize the preparation of crucial |T> magic states for fault-tolerant quantum computing. It dynamically balances cultivation and distillation by treating the total error budget as a shared resource. By co-optimizing these processes, the method significantly outperforms static baselines in terms of speed and resource efficiency.
main_problem: Magic |T> state preparation is the most resource-intensive step in fault-tolerant quantum computation using surface codes, and existing methods fail to optimally balance fidelity, resource usage, and a total error budget.
main_result: The proposed Gap-Priced |T> States (GP|T>S) scheduler achieves significant speedups (up to 5.5x) and volume reductions (up to 3.4x) across various benchmarks while strictly adhering to a user-defined total T-error budget.
method: The authors developed a co-optimization framework using dynamic programming to jointly schedule dynamic cultivation post-selection (based on the complementary gap) and allocate distillation factories across a catalog, all constrained by the total error budget.
model_or_system: The work is situated in the context of Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation (FTQC) using the surface code, focusing specifically on the preparation of magic |T> states via lattice surgery.
key_observables: Logical cycle count, space-time volume, and the total T-error budget ($\epsilon$).
important_parameters: Total T-error budget ($\epsilon$), cultivation gap cutoff, and factory size/rate.
main_assumptions: Existing schedulers are budget-agnostic, and static allocation methods cannot optimally balance the trade-off between fidelity and speed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dynamic adjustment of the gap cutoff and the co-optimization process, comparing the proposed method against cultivation-only and single-factory baselines across multiple benchmarks.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the core problem, details the GP|T>S methodology (dynamic post-selection and factory allocation), presents the optimization framework using dynamic programming, and validates the approach across sixteen benchmarks under varying error budgets.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the resource management aspect—co-optimizing multiple competing resource requirements (time vs. space vs. error)—is highly relevant to any field dealing with complex, constrained physical simulations or experimental setups.

Figure 3. Where this work sits relative to existing FTQC methods. Current lattice surgery schedulers are budget- agnostic, meaning that while they boast short execution times, they do not perform any resource estimation that would otherwise bottleneck practical, on-hardware execu- tion. At the other end, static allocation of a stringent gap cutoff, or of an unwieldy and large distillation factory, can both execute under budget, but at significant time cost.
